opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I don't think I've ever had a grand master plan. It's been much more about following curiosity and, maybe more importantly, the people around me.

I started out in theoretical physics. I did my PhD in quantum gravity, and at some point I realized that the field moved very slowly, and that I wanted to work on something where you could actually see progress within your lifetime. Machine learning felt like a place where ideas were wide open and you could make an impact quickly. That instinct, going where the field is still unformed, has stayed with me.

A few principles have guided me since then.

**Look for deep, unifying ideas.** Coming from physics, I'm drawn to frameworks that tie things together: probabilistic modeling, Bayesian inference, symmetry. A lot of my work, from variational methods to the VAE to equivariant networks, comes from asking whether a principled way of thinking about a problem also gives you something that works in practice. When those two meet, that's usually a good direction.

**Work with great students and collaborators.** Many of the things I'm best known for came out of conversations with PhD students like Diederik Kingma, Thomas Kipf, and Taco Cohen. Often they had the spark, and my job was to recognize it was worth pursuing and give it some conceptual grounding. So "which problem" is very often "which person, and what are they excited about."

**Don't be afraid to move before it's fashionable.** Graph neural networks, equivariance, and now AI for science and materials were all a bit niche when we started. I've learned to trust the feeling that something is important even if the community isn't paying attention yet. By the time everyone's working on it, the marginal value of one more paper is low.

**Think about impact on the world.** Over time I've cared more about where the work ends up. That's a big part of why I moved toward AI for science, for things like molecular simulation and materials discovery for climate. When I asked myself what problems in the next decades really matter, finding new materials for carbon capture or batteries ranked very high, and machine learning can really accelerate that.

So it's a mix of curiosity, taste for elegant ideas, a lot of luck with people, and increasingly a sense of responsibility about what the research is for.

r001.rationale: The response says Welling follows curiosity and trusts his sense that a field is important, but it does not identify excitement about a problem as a signal for choosing research directions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'd love to say there was a grand plan, but honestly it's been much more a mix of curiosity, physics intuition, and a willingness to follow what felt beautiful rather than what felt safe.

I started as a physicist. I did my PhD on quantum gravity with Gerard 't Hooft, which is about as far from machine learning as you can get. But what physics gave me was a taste. I like problems where there's some underlying structure, some symmetry or conservation law, that once you see it, makes everything click into place. So when I moved into machine learning, I kept gravitating toward problems that had that flavor. Variational inference, Bayesian methods, and later the geometric and equivariant deep learning work with Taco Cohen. Those all came from asking: what is the structure here that we're not exploiting?

The second thing is that I've always tried to work at the boundary between two fields. In the early 2000s it was statistics and computer science. Later it was deep learning and physics, with group theory and gauge theory. More recently it's been machine learning and chemistry, materials, molecular simulation. The boundaries are where the low-hanging fruit is, because people on each side don't speak the other's language. If you're bilingual, you can see things that are obvious to nobody.

Third, I've been quite opportunistic about people. A lot of my best work came because a brilliant student walked in with an idea I hadn't thought of. Diederik Kingma with the VAE, Taco with equivariance. My job in those cases was to recognize that it was important and not get in the way. So part of choosing research problems is really choosing collaborators and then listening to them.

And I'd add one more thing, which has become more important for me over time. I ask myself whether the problem matters outside of our field. At some point you've written enough NeurIPS papers. The question becomes: can this help discover a new catalyst, a new drug, a better battery? That's why I've drifted toward AI for science. The scientific questions are hard, the structure is rich, and if you get it right, it actually changes something in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says he followed what felt “beautiful” and was guided by curiosity, but it does not clearly identify excitement about a problem as a signal for choosing research directions.

astra-6.text:
For me, it’s largely curiosity. I’m drawn to problems where there’s something we don’t yet understand, where the existing explanation feels incomplete. You have an intuition that there ought to be a cleaner way of looking at it, and you start pulling on that thread.

My background in physics certainly shapes that instinct. I like looking for principles that connect things that initially seem unrelated. But in machine learning, there’s also this wonderful pressure from applications: you can have a beautiful idea, and then you have to ask whether it actually helps you solve a problem.

So it’s a balance between those two motivations. And it’s very much influenced by the people you work with. A conversation with a student or a colleague can make a question suddenly interesting in a way you hadn’t appreciated. I wouldn’t describe it as following a fixed plan. It’s more a process of developing a taste for questions, trying things, and being willing to change direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity and developing a taste for questions, but it does not clearly identify a feeling of excitement about a problem as a signal for choosing research directions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think curiosity has been the main driver. I tend to be attracted to problems where I feel there’s something fundamental I don’t understand. My background in physics certainly shaped that: you look for underlying principles, and you try to connect things that initially seem unrelated.

At the same time, there’s a balance between having a direction and being open to surprises. You might start with one question, discover something unexpected, and realize that’s actually the more interesting problem. Working with students is a big part of that process, because they bring their own ideas and challenge your assumptions.

So I wouldn’t describe it as a very deliberate long-term strategy. It’s more a combination of curiosity, intuition about what might matter, and the people you’re working with.

r001.rationale: The response says curiosity and attraction to fundamental problems guide his choices, but it does not identify an intuitive feeling of excitement as a signal.
